content: Wee1 is a nuclear kinase that belongs to the Serine/Threonine family of protein kinases in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe (S. pombe). It has a molecular mass of 96 kDa and plays a critical role in regulating cell cycle progression. Wee1 influences cell size by inhibiting the entry into mitosis through the inhibition of Cdk1. Homologues of Wee1 are found in many other organisms, including mammals. The regulation of cell size is essential for maintaining cellular functionality. In addition to environmental factors such as nutrient availability, growth factors, and functional load, cell size is controlled by an intrinsic cellular checkpoint. Wee1 is a key component of this checkpoint, determining the timing of mitotic entry and thereby influencing the size of daughter cells. Loss of Wee1 function results in smaller-than-normal daughter cells due to premature cell division. The name Wee1 originates from the Scottish dialect word wee, meaning small, as its discoverer, Paul Nurse, was working at the University of Edinburgh in Scotland at the time of its discovery. Wee1 inhibits Cdk1 by phosphorylating it at two specific sites, Tyrosine 15 (Tyr15) and Threonine 14 (Thr14). Cdk1 is essential for the cyclin-dependent progression through various cell cycle checkpoints. At least three checkpoints rely on Wee1-mediated inhibition of Cdk1: 1. G2/M Checkpoint: Wee1 phosphorylates Tyr15 and Thr14 of Cdk1, keeping its kinase activity low and preventing mitotic entry. In S. pombe, this allows further cell growth. The inactivation of Cdk1 by Wee1 is highly sensitive due to substrate competition. During mitotic entry, Wee1 activity is reduced by several regulators, leading to increased Cdk1 activity. In S. pombe, the protein kinase Pom1 localizes to the cell poles and activates a pathway in which Cdr2 inhibits Wee1 via Cdr1. Additionally, Cdk1 itself negatively regulates Wee1 through phosphorylation, creating a positive feedback loop. However, decreased Wee1 activity alone is insufficient for mitotic entry; cyclin synthesis and activating phosphorylation by a Cdk-activating kinase (CAK) are also required. 2. Cell Size Checkpoint: Evidence suggests the existence of a cell size checkpoint that prevents small cells from entering mitosis. Wee1 plays a role in this checkpoint by coordinating cell size with cell cycle progression. 3. DNA Damage Checkpoint: This checkpoint also regulates the G2/M transition. In S. pombe, it delays mitotic entry in cells with DNA damage (e.g., caused by gamma radiation). The lengthening of the G2 phase depends on Wee1, as wee1 mutants do not exhibit a prolonged G2 phase after gamma irradiation. Additionally, Wee1 has been reported to have an epigenetic function, phosphorylating histone H2B at tyrosine 37, which regulates global histone expression. The WEE1 gene has two known homologues in humans: WEE1 (also known as WEE1A) and WEE2 (WEE1B). The corresponding proteins, Wee1-like protein kinase and Wee1-like protein kinase 2, act on the human Cdk1 homologue. In budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), the homologue of Wee1 is called Swe1. In S. pombe, Wee1 phosphorylates Cdk1, which, along with cyclin B, forms the maturation-promoting factor (MPF) that drives mitotic entry. MPF is inactivated by Wee1-mediated phosphorylation and activated by the phosphatase Cdc25C. Cdc25C is itself activated by Polo kinase and inactivated by Chk1. Thus, Wee1 regulation in S. pombe is primarily controlled by phosphorylation through the Pom1 pathway, which includes Cdr2 and Cdr1. At the G2/M transition, Cdk1 is activated by Cdc25 through dephosphorylation of Tyr15, while Wee1 is inactivated by phosphorylation at its C-terminal catalytic domain by Nim1/Cdr1. Active MPF further promotes its own activity by activating Cdc25 and inactivating Wee1, creating a positive feedback loop, though the details of this mechanism are not fully understood. In higher eukaryotes, Wee1 is regulated through phosphorylation and degradation. The SCFβ-TrCP1/2 protein complex, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, mediates Wee1A ubiquitination. M-phase kinases such as Polo-like kinase (Plk1) and Cdc2 phosphorylate two serine residues in Wee1A, which are recognized by SCFβ-TrCP1/2. In S. cerevisiae, the homologue Swe1 phosphorylates Cdk28 (the Cdk1 homologue) and is dephosphorylated by Mih1 (the Cdc25 homologue). The Nim1/Cdr1 homologue in S. cerevisiae, Hsl1, along with related kinases Gin4 and Kcc4, localizes Swe1 to the bud neck. Bud-neck-associated kinases Cla4 and Cdc5 (Polo kinase homologue) phosphorylate Swe1 at different stages of the cell cycle. Swe1 is also phosphorylated by Clb2-Cdk28, which serves as a recognition signal for further phosphorylation by Cdc5. Swe1 is regulated by degradation, as hyperphosphorylation by Clb2-Cdk28 and Cdc5 may signal ubiquitination and degradation by the SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, similar to higher eukaryotes. Wee1 also plays a role in cancer. The mitosis-promoting factor (MPF) regulates DNA damage-induced apoptosis. Negative regulation of MPF by WEE1 leads to aberrant mitosis and resistance to DNA damage-induced apoptosis. Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) negatively regulates human WEE1, thereby increasing sensitivity to DNA damage-induced apoptosis in cancer cells. Wee1 acts as a dosage-dependent inhibitor of mitosis. The amount of Wee1 protein correlates with cell size. In fission yeast, the wee1 mutant (also called wee1−) divides at a significantly smaller cell size than wild-type cells. Since Wee1 inhibits mitotic entry, its absence leads to premature division and sub-normal cell size. Conversely, increased Wee1 expression delays mitosis, allowing cells to grow to a larger size before dividing.
